astra.text:
Yeah, I think there is something fundamental about language. Language is how we, we communicate knowledge, right? We use language to explain things, to describe problems, to write down how we solve those problems. So when you train on language, you have this opportunity to learn from a lot of human knowledge across very different domains, using the same interface.

And I think language is already a kind of abstraction. With an image, you have all these details, but it’s not necessarily clear which details matter, or what you want the model to do with them. With language, people have already done some of that work. They have selected something to describe, or organized an explanation. So my intuition is that this makes the data particularly useful for learning capabilities that people care about.

But there’s also the interaction part. You can tell the model what you want, in the same language you use to talk to another person. That’s a very powerful interface, because different users can bring very different tasks to the same model. With a vision model that only classifies images, the task is already fixed, right?

So I would say it’s both the knowledge in the data and the flexibility of the interface. Vision being a natural bridge between sensory modalities doesn’t necessarily mean vision alone gives us the easiest way to build a useful assistant. I think language provides that connection to what the user actually wants. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think there is something fundamental there. Vision may be the default input for perception, but language is the default interface for knowledge and for communicating intent. A user can describe almost any task in language—write code, summarize a paper, plan a trip, explain a concept—and the model can also return the result through the same interface. So you don't need to build a separate system or user interface for every task. You just talk to it.

And language data on the internet contains much more than words. It contains compressed human knowledge, reasoning processes, instructions, code, discussions, and descriptions of the visual and physical world. Predicting the next token on sufficiently broad data therefore forces the model to learn many underlying structures. Vision data is extremely rich, but an image by itself often doesn't tell you what task should be performed or which aspects are important. Language provides that abstraction and supervision.

So I think the jump came from several things together: the scale and diversity of text data, the fact that language connects many different domains, and the very low barrier for users to interact with the model. It is not that vision was unimportant. Vision gives models access to the world, and it can serve as a bridge among modalities, as we discussed. But language became the central interface—the place where perception, knowledge, reasoning, and action could all meet. Once the language models became good enough to follow instructions, suddenly the same model became useful to almost everyone, and that made the progress much more visible.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I don't think it's a coincidence. I think there is something fundamental there, and, and it's maybe two or three things.

So the first one is that language is already, kind of a compressed, abstracted representation of human knowledge, right? It's, it's a human invention specifically designed for, for transmitting concepts between people. So when you train on text, you are not learning from raw sensory signal, you are learning from something that humans have already, done the abstraction for you. Whereas in vision, pixels contain a huge amount of information that is just, not semantic at all, like lighting, texture, and, and we spend most of our capacity modeling that.

And the second one, which I think is maybe even more important, is the interface. in, in vision, for a long time, we didn't have a universal task. We had classification with 1,000 categories, we had detection, segmentation, and each of them is a, is a narrow interface with its own output head, right? And, and you finish ImageNet, and then, then what? Whereas language has this property that every task can be written as text in, text out. So question answering, translation, coding, summarization, they, they're all the same interface. And that, that means one model can absorb everything, and also it, it means next token prediction is a, is a self-supervised objective that's, that's extremely rich and well-defined. In vision, our self-supervised objectives have always been a bit, awkward, right? Like, what does it mean to predict the next patch? It's, it's not as natural.

And, and then thirdly, just, the product side. People interact with, with each other through language. So if a model can speak language, everyone immediately knows how to use it, there's no, no learning curve. And a lot of, economically valuable work is, is basically text in, text out.

So I, I would say language got there first because it had the cleanest interface and the, the most distilled data. But I don't think vision is, is fundamentally behind. I think it just, it joined later, through this, tokenization into the language model's space. And, and I would guess video and, and embodied data is, is where the next, jump comes from, but, that's, that's much harder data to get. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah, I, I don’t think this is a coincidence. I think there is something pretty fundamental about language.

So, vision is extremely important, right? We just talked about ImageBind, and I still think vision is this natural bridge across modalities, because so many other signals co-occur with images and video. But the jump in capabilities, and especially the jump in adoption, I would say, came through language because language is the interface. It’s how we specify goals, how we store knowledge, how we reason out loud, how we teach, how we write code, how we talk to other people. Once the model can do that well, suddenly everybody has a way to use it. You don’t need to be a vision researcher with a detection pipeline. You can just, like, talk to it.

For a long time, vision models were already quite strong on specific tasks, classifying, detecting, segmenting. But the interaction was not general. You train a model for a task, you get an output for that task. Language models, once they got good enough, became this general-purpose interface. You can ask them almost anything, and they can, they can chain skills together in a way that looks much more like how people actually want to use AI at work, in products, in daily life. That’s why companies suddenly started using it. It’s not only that the numbers went up. The interface matched human communication.

And then, on the training side, I do think language is an unusually rich signal. Next-token prediction on internet-scale text is covering so many things at once: knowledge, reasoning, dialogue, coding, instructions. A lot of the “intelligence” people care about is already written down in language. Vision data is huge too, but a lot of it is more about appearance and perception, and unless you have the right paired language, it doesn’t automatically teach the model how to, how to be useful in this open-ended way.

The other piece, going back to what I said earlier about transformers and LLaVA-style models, is that once you have a strong language model, everything else can be converted into tokens and plugged in. Vision encoder, audio, tools, memory. Language became the backbone, the thing other modalities align to. So vision was there, and it still matters a lot, but language was the thing that made the system general, and that made it usable by a much broader set of people. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I don't think it's a coincidence. I think language has a few very unique, fundamental properties compared to vision.

First, language is inherently high-level and dense in information. In vision, when you look at an image or a video, there are millions of pixels, but most of them are redundant—it's just background, lighting changes, textures, noise. The actual semantic concept in an image is quite sparse. But language is already a distilled, abstract representation of human thought, knowledge, and reasoning. Every word, every token carries high semantic meaning. So when you train on internet-scale text, you are directly training on distilled human knowledge, logic, and reasoning steps.

And second, I think language is a universal interface. In computer vision, historically we fragmented tasks into very specific problem formulations—like ImageNet classification, object detection with bounding boxes, semantic segmentation masks. Each task had its own specialized architecture, output heads, and metrics, which makes it hard to generalize and hard for ordinary people to interact with. But with language, it's just text-in, text-out. You can cast almost any human task—answering questions, writing code, summarizing, translating, reasoning—into next-token prediction. And that makes it immediately usable for anyone in the world through a simple chat interface.

So I think language provided both the right level of abstraction for reasoning to emerge, and the natural interface for people to actually interact with AI directly. Vision is crucial for perception and grounding, but language is really the vehicle for thought and communication.

kimi.text:
Yeah. Yeah, no, I don't think it's a coincidence. I, I do think there's something fundamental in language. I would say there are a few, a few reasons.

One is that language is, is kind of the natural interface, between humans and, and, and machines, right? even before AI, we have been communicating with computers through language, through command lines, through code, which is, like, a written formal language. So if you want, a model that people can, can instruct, can give tasks to in a very flexible way, language is kind of the, the default protocol. vision models, they, they perception, they do perception, right? they, they classify, they detect. but, but perceiving is not the same as, as communicating or, taking instructions. So the, the jump in adoption, I think, happened when the model became something you can talk to, you can, can ask anything in, in natural language.

The second reason, I think, is, is data again. language data is, is the easiest to collect at internet scale, and it comes with a, a very natural self-supervision signal, which is next token prediction. you don't need labels at all. whereas vision, for a long time, relied on, on labeled datasets like ImageNet, which are, very expensive, to annotate. so the scale of vision data was limited by human labeling effort, while for language, you can just, scrape the internet and, and the supervision is built in. So the, the scaling happened first there.

And I think there's another point about information density. like, text is, is a very compressed, very dense representation of, of human knowledge and, and reasoning. images and videos have a lot of, of redundancy, a lot of pixels that don't carry much information. So per unit of compute, you, you kind of gain more knowledge from, from text.

And the last thing is, language solved the, the task unification problem. In vision, we used to have different models with different heads for classification, detection, segmentation. but in language, translation, question answering, coding, reasoning, they are all just text in, text out. so once the model gets good at, at this one unified task, it, it implicitly gets good at everything that, that has been written down by humans. So that, that generality is, is what makes the jump.

But that being said, I do think vision and other modalities are now, catching up, exactly through this framework we talked about, where language is the backbone and, and other modalities get, get plugged in as tokens. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a, that's a great question. I, I think it's not a coincidence. I, I think there is something fundamental there. so, so a few things. first, language is the, is the natural interface for, for humans, right? It's, it's how we, we communicate, how we give instructions, how we ask questions. So, so when the model gets good at language, it directly becomes useful to, to everybody, because everybody can, can just talk to it. Whereas in vision, for, for a long time, our models are, are more like, perception models, right? You give an image, it gives you a label, or a bounding box, or a segmentation mask. It's very useful for, for some applications, self-driving, medical, but, but it's not something an ordinary person will, will interact with every day. There's no, there's no output space that, that people can, like, directly consume. so the interface matters a lot for, for adoption.

And secondly, I, I think it's about the data. Text on the internet is, is kind of a, a compressed record of, of human knowledge, right? People write things down deliberately. It, it's, it has, reasoning, it has explanations, it has, procedures. It's, it's very information dense compared to, to images. If you, if you take a random image from the internet, most of the pixels are, are kind of redundant, and they don't tell you much about, about how the world works, at, at a, at an abstract level. But a random paragraph from Wikipedia, it, it tells you a lot. So, so per, per bit, or per, per, token, language is, is just a, a much richer supervision signal. And, and I think also the, the training objective, next token prediction, is, it's so simple and, and so natural for, for discrete tokens. In vision, we, we struggled for, for many years to find the right self-supervised objective, right? Contrastive learning, masked image modeling, they, they work to some extent, but they, they never gave us the same kind of, emergent, general abilities that, that next word prediction gave us in, in language. and, and I think it's because, predicting the next word, requires you to, to model, kind of the, the, the thoughts behind the text, not just the surface. Predicting the next pixel, doesn't require that as much.

So, so I, I guess, back to the ImageBind story, vision is, is a good bridge for, for aligning modalities, because it co-occurs with, with everything. But language is, is the, the hub for, for, for reasoning and for, for interfacing with people. And, and in fact, now most of the, the vision progress is, is, is also going through language, right? Multimodal models, they, they encode the image into, into tokens and, and let the language model do the, the thinking and the, the talking. So, so even for vision, the, the useful capability comes out, through language. I, I think that's, that's pretty fundamental, at least in, in the, in the current paradigm. Yeah.
